title: Validating Script Arguments knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Validating Script Arguments”?
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Checking argument count” under lesson 79, “Validating Script Arguments”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Validating Script Arguments”?
options: Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Validate inputs, define usage, and keep machine-readable output separate from diagnostics.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs, define usage, and keep machine-readable output separate from diagnostics.
questions.explanation: Validate inputs, define usage, and keep machine-readable output separate from diagnostics. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Validating Script Arguments”?
options: Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters.
questions.answer_key: Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters.
questions.explanation: Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
